title: The TOBA as a training ground in respect and fidelity
summary: He describes the TOBA circuit's route and the code of looking after sick or stranded performers, and recalls helping James P. Johnson and Willie the Lion later.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: It was a very interesting training ground. It was like a Who's Who in America, you know, in black America because if they were anybody, from Georgie Williams and Bessie Brown to Bert Williams to Ma Rainey to Trixie Smith to...well, Ella wasn't around in those days, you know...you know this TOBA was way before. And Joe Bright, and you had...and most of these towns that they played were towns in the Southwest, starting, for example...they had like a circuit, and you'd start in...occasionally in Chicago, but mostly in St. Louis to Kansas City and Kansas City to Tulsa, Tulsa to Oklahoma City, Oklahoma City to Dallas, Dallas to Houston, Houston to Galveston, Galveston to Shreveport, Shreveport to Mobile, Mobile to Atlanta. Then you had Norfolk, and then usually the shows would break up in Washington. You had maybe 15 weeks. But it was very, very interesting/and Dan, the thing that it taught you--and I still have that same fidelity today, that I have a lot of respect for artists and I demand that they have it for me. And I'm very, very sensitive about that...that's one of the things that I learned on that show...is a respect for each other. For example, if a guy is sick, and he lived in Houston, and we were in Tulsa, we'd take care of him in Tulsa, Oklahoma City, Dallas, and on the fourth week we'd deliver him to his people in Houston. If you wanted to send

some money you'd say, 'Now, when you get down in Shreveport, give this to my aunt and stay with her that week.' And maybe coming from the other way, Louisville, you come back down to Winston-Salem and back down and all until you get to Shreveport and you give the money to the parent or the mother of the friend, and so forth. So, I think that, that one thing that that thing taught you was fidelity, friendship and respect and recognition. Now we don't practice that all the time, that's an important fact. For example, I may pan some guy, you know, that's human nature to talk about a guy behind his back, though when you're with him...you know what I mean...when you're with him you don't really mean it, you're just running your mouth. And of all the piano players that I've played with, I don't really say that a guy can't play. I may not like it, but I've come into some great music... great piano players, you know...Donald Lambert, you know, James P. Johnson. One year when I was successful in New York and was working for Decca I had an office at 1674 Broadway. You know that I gave Willie the Lion Smith and James P. Johnson an office with a piano where they could come every day and, you know, and practice, and I did it just because...out of respect for them. And then I helped to promote James P.'s 'Yamacraw' at Carnegie Hall. And I always

have been like that with musicians, that I would share what I have, like I knew how to...well, I won't say I knew how to get money from women, but I knew...well, you know, women liked me and they would want to do me favors, and if some guy...you understand, Dan, wasn't doing too well, he could always come to me. That guy was here, right here. One time I owed my rent...my rent was a thousand dollars and his rent was a hundred and I had a hundred dollars. And you know what I did? I gave it to him. He paid his rent. 'Cause all they could do was evict me, you know what I mean, and by the time they'd evict me, I'd hustle the money. But I always...Eddie Barefield always said that every town that I went in over the years, Sam Price was always sure with a woman. (Laughter). He say, "You've always got a woman with you." I said well there was a reason for that. You know, she's probably buying the tickets. (Laughter.) But the TOBA was quite a training ground for things that were later to come.
